name: Tongue thrust correction

lead: Tongue thrust is a swallowing pattern in which the tongue pushes forward against or between the front teeth instead of lifting to the palate. Correcting it is meant to stop that repeated pressure so the teeth sit straighter, open bites close or stay closed, and orthodontic results hold.

Clinicians describe a link between tongue thrust and malocclusion such as open bite and protruding front teeth, though reviews note the cause-and-effect direction is debated. Treatment reviews describe exercise-based therapy and habit-breaking appliances as promising, with calls for more research.

paras: The usual route is orofacial myofunctional therapy led by a speech-language pathologist or dentist: exercises for tongue awareness, tongue resting position, lip closure and a mature swallow, practised at home over months. Orthodontists may add a tongue crib, tongue spurs or a soft tongue restrainer, and may also address mouth breathing or thumb sucking if present.

The exercises themselves are low-risk. Appliances such as cribs or spurs can cause temporary speech changes, soreness or eating difficulty and are fitted by a dentist. Results depend on consistent practice, and a thrusting pattern can contribute to relapse after braces according to the literature, which is why clinicians often treat it alongside orthodontics.

angle.text: Correction aims to remove a repeated forward force on the front teeth. Clinicians use it alongside or ahead of braces to help teeth end up aligned and stay there; the change in appearance comes through the teeth and bite rather than through the tongue itself.

lead: Tongue thrust, also called reverse swallow or atypical swallowing, is a pattern in which the tongue presses forward against or between the teeth when swallowing, speaking or resting. Tongue thrust correction is the set of methods used to change that pattern: awareness training, myofunctional exercises, and sometimes orthodontic appliances. [1][2][3]

People pursue it for how it affects the teeth and lower face. Reviews associate tongue thrusting with anterior open bite, protruded front teeth and other malocclusion patterns, and note that a non-physiological tongue thrust can interfere with orthodontic treatment in progress. Correcting the habit is therefore described as a way to support straighter teeth and a stable bite, and in looksmaxxing discussion it overlaps with talk of tongue posture and facial development. [2][4][5]

Research is mostly reviews and small clinical studies. A 2024 systematic review found that orofacial myofunctional therapy, tongue cribs, habit-correcting appliances and soft tongue restrainers were all reported as potential therapies, while concluding that more research is required. [6]

paras: In a mature swallow the tongue lifts against the palate and the bolus moves backward without pressing on the teeth. In tongue thrust the tongue moves forward against or between the teeth, and the pattern may also occur at rest or during speech. It reflects the infantile swallow persisting beyond the age when most children transition to a mature pattern. [1][7]

Suggested contributors include prolonged thumb sucking or pacifier use, enlarged adenoids or tonsils, mouth breathing and a large tongue; the Wikipedia article notes that evidence on causes is weak and that some authors regard the pattern as an adaptive lip-seal mechanism rather than a disorder. [1][7][1]

Estimates of how common it is vary widely by age and study. A 2025 meta-analysis of oral habits in children aged 3 to 18 pooled 54 studies, and listed tongue thrusting among the habits that contribute to dentofacial anomalies. [5]

A 2014 review of atypical swallowing examined the connection with malocclusion. It reported that the relationship appears to run both ways: some authors hold that the habit begins as compensation for an existing open bite, while others hold that it worsens malocclusion, and that a non-physiological tongue thrust can negatively affect ongoing orthodontic therapy. [2]

A 2024 review of oral habits in children describes an established association between tongue thrusting, thumb sucking and mouth breathing and patterns including anterior open bite, proclination, crowding and posterior crossbite. [4] Wikipedia notes that the link to malocclusion is disputed and that some studies found no clear difference in speech outcomes. [7]

Orofacial myofunctional therapy (OMT) is a programme of exercises aimed at tongue awareness, tongue posture, lip seal and a mature swallow. A 2021 narrative review describes several OMT exercises that can be done at home under parental supervision and reports a positive influence on affected patients, advising early detection and removal of underlying causes such as enlarged adenoids. [3]

Orthodontic appliances are used to break the habit while teeth and bite are corrected. The 2024 systematic review of 12 studies on atypical swallowing and malocclusion named OMT, the crib appliance, the Habit Corrector and soft tongue restrainers as potential therapies and reported effective clinical outcomes, while stating that more research is needed. [6]

A 2025 randomized clinical study compared tongue tamers and customized bonded spurs as early treatment of anterior open bite. [8] Wikipedia notes that appliances work best during growth and may take up to about six months. [7]

Human research includes a 2004 ultrasound study comparing tongue function in mature and tongue-thrust swallowing, [9] the 2025 randomized trial of tongue tamers and bonded spurs in open bite, [8] and a randomized trial of functional chewing training for tongue thrust and drooling in children with cerebral palsy. [10] The systematic review of 12 studies concluded that several approaches produce clinical improvement but that the evidence base is small and further research is needed. [6]

In appearance communities the topic is generally folded into discussion of tongue posture and jaw or facial development, with adults interested in whether swallowing habits affect their bite and profile. Published studies concern mainly children with malocclusion and do not address facial-structure claims in adults.
